phrases.cultural_note: 'Ayubowan' and 'Vanakkam' mean 'may you live long.' Often accompanied by a slight bow and palms pressed together.
phrases.usage_tips: Formal greeting suitable for any occasion. Shows respect and cultural awareness.

phrases.cultural_note: Used from sunrise until around 10 AM.
phrases.usage_tips: Perfect for greeting shop owners, hotel staff, or locals you meet in the morning.

phrases.cultural_note: Used from around 4 PM onwards.
phrases.usage_tips: Great for evening greetings at restaurants or when meeting people after work hours.

phrases.cultural_note: Used when parting in the evening or before sleep.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this when leaving a restaurant at night or when checking into your hotel.

phrases.cultural_note: Common casual greeting. Expect 'Hari hondai' (I'm fine) as a response.
phrases.usage_tips: Use with people you've met before or in casual conversations.

phrases.pronunciation: HA-ri, bo-HO-ma sthu-thi / naan nan-draa-ga i-ruk-ki-ren nan-dri
phrases.cultural_note: Standard polite response to 'How are you?'
phrases.usage_tips: Always respond with this to show politeness and respect.

phrases.cultural_note: One of the most important phrases. Locals appreciate gratitude.
phrases.usage_tips: Use frequently! After receiving help, service, or gifts.

phrases.cultural_note: In Sinhala, 'please' usually comes at the beginning of requests, not the end.
phrases.usage_tips: Essential for polite requests. Shows respect and good manners.

phrases.cultural_note: Use to apologize or get someone's attention politely.
phrases.usage_tips: Essential before asking for directions or interrupting someone.

phrases.pronunciation: o-yaa in-gri-si ka-thaa ka-ra-na-wa-da / neen-gal aan-gi-lam pe-su-veer-ga-la
phrases.cultural_note: Many Sri Lankans speak at least basic English, especially in tourist areas.
phrases.usage_tips: Use this before launching into complex questions.

phrases.cultural_note: Honesty is appreciated. People will often find someone who speaks English to help.
phrases.usage_tips: Don't be shy to use this. It helps avoid misunderstandings.

phrases.pronunciation: sæn-ta ka-thaa ka-ran-na / me-dhu pe-sa ven-dum
phrases.cultural_note: People will happily slow down for you.
phrases.usage_tips: Combine with 'I don't understand' when struggling with fast speech.

phrases.cultural_note: Response to 'thank you.' Often accompanied by a smile.
phrases.usage_tips: Use after someone thanks you for help or service.

phrases.cultural_note: Casual way to say goodbye, literally 'going and coming.'
phrases.usage_tips: Use with people you'll likely see again soon.

phrases.cultural_note: Always add 'please' (karunakarala) before asking.
phrases.usage_tips: Point to a map or show a written location name for clarity.

phrases.cultural_note: Distances may be given in kilometers or travel time.
phrases.usage_tips: Have your destination name ready in both English and local script.

phrases.cultural_note: Left and right directions are clear, but 'straight' might need gestures.
phrases.usage_tips: Watch for hand gestures that accompany verbal directions.

phrases.cultural_note: Right turns are common in Sri Lankan traffic flow.
phrases.usage_tips: Confirm direction by pointing or repeating back what you heard.

phrases.cultural_note: 'Straight' might be accompanied by pointing gestures.
phrases.usage_tips: Look for landmarks mentioned along with directions.

phrases.cultural_note: 'Near' often means within walking distance in Sri Lankan context.
phrases.usage_tips: Clarify if something is walkable or requires transport.

phrases.english: Can you show me on the map?
phrases.pronunciation: si-thi-ya-men pen-wan-na pu-lu-wan-da / va-rai-pa-da-thil kaat-ta mu-di-yu-maa
phrases.cultural_note: Locals are very helpful and will often draw maps for you.
phrases.usage_tips: Have Google Maps ready on your phone to show and confirm.

phrases.cultural_note: Polite way to order. Point to menu items if pronunciation is difficult.
phrases.usage_tips: Follow with the dish name or point to the menu.

phrases.pronunciation: ra-sa næ / a-du ra-sa / kaa-ram ven-daam / ku-rain-dha kaa-ram
phrases.cultural_note: Sri Lankan food can be very spicy. Don't be shy about asking for less spice!
phrases.usage_tips: Emphasize this BEFORE ordering if you prefer mild food.

phrases.cultural_note: If you love spice, locals will be impressed!
phrases.usage_tips: Say this if you want authentic Sri Lankan spice levels.

phrases.cultural_note: Vegetarian food is common and well-understood in Sri Lanka.
phrases.usage_tips: Many rice and curry options are naturally vegetarian.

phrases.cultural_note: Always ask for bottled water for safety.
phrases.usage_tips: Specify 'bottle water' to ensure sealed bottled water.

phrases.pronunciation: bi-la e-ka gen-na-ko / bill tha-ya-vu sei-thu
phrases.cultural_note: Service charge is often included. Tipping is not mandatory but appreciated.
phrases.usage_tips: Make eye contact with server and use this phrase or the hand-writing gesture.

phrases.cultural_note: Compliment the cook! They'll appreciate it.
phrases.usage_tips: Use this to show appreciation after a good meal.

phrases.cultural_note: Bargaining is expected in markets but not in fixed-price shops.
phrases.usage_tips: Always ask the price before committing to buy.

phrases.cultural_note: Start negotiating around 30-40% of the asking price.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this with a smile to start bargaining conversation.

phrases.pronunciation: mi-la a-du ka-ran-na pu-lu-wan-da / vi-lai-yai ku-raik-ka mu-di-yu-maa
phrases.cultural_note: Polite way to bargain. Be friendly and patient.
phrases.usage_tips: Use after expressing interest in an item.

phrases.cultural_note: Make your counter-offer clearly and wait for response.
phrases.usage_tips: State your price and be prepared to meet in the middle.

phrases.pronunciation: an-thi-ma mi-la mo-kad-da / i-ru-dhi vi-lai en-na
phrases.cultural_note: Ask this when you're ready to close the deal.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this after a few rounds of bargaining.

phrases.cultural_note: Say this when you've agreed on a price.
phrases.usage_tips: Be firm once you commit to buying.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma ba-lan-na vi-tha-rai / naan paar-ki-ren mat-tu-me
phrases.cultural_note: Vendors may be persistent. Be polite but firm.
phrases.usage_tips: Use this to browse without pressure to buy.

phrases.cultural_note: People will respond quickly to cries for help.
phrases.usage_tips: Shout loudly in emergencies. Don't hesitate.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ta vai-dya-wa-rek o-ni / e-nak-ku ma-rut-thu-var ven-dum
phrases.cultural_note: Hospitals and clinics are widely available. Ask for 'private hospital' for better facilities.
phrases.usage_tips: Specify if it's urgent. Hotels can call doctors.

phrases.cultural_note: Tourist police (119) speak English and are very helpful.
phrases.usage_tips: Know the emergency number 119 for police.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma a-tha-ra-ma-ga we-la / naan tho-lain-thu po-nen
phrases.cultural_note: Don't panic. Locals are very helpful to lost tourists.
phrases.usage_tips: Show your hotel address or destination on your phone.

phrases.cultural_note: Private hospitals have better facilities than government hospitals.
phrases.usage_tips: Ask for directions or call a taxi immediately.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ta sa-nee-pa næ / e-nak-ku u-dal-ni-lai sa-ri-yil-lai
phrases.cultural_note: Common issues include heat exhaustion and food sensitivity.
phrases.usage_tips: Describe symptoms if possible or point to where it hurts.

phrases.cultural_note: Use this word to emphasize urgency.
phrases.usage_tips: Combine with other phrases to convey serious situations.

phrases.pronunciation: bas na-wa-thum stha-na-ya ko-he-da / pe-run-dhu ni-rut-tham en-ge
phrases.cultural_note: Buses are the cheapest way to travel. Bus stops aren't always marked.
phrases.usage_tips: Ask locals or look for groups of people waiting.

phrases.pronunciation: me bas e-ka ya-na-wa-da / in-dha pe-run-dhu sel-lu-maa
phrases.cultural_note: Bus destinations are often in Sinhala or Tamil only.
phrases.usage_tips: Show your destination written down or on a map.

phrases.cultural_note: Agree on fare before getting into tuk-tuks or taxis without meters.
phrases.usage_tips: Negotiate tuk-tuk fares before starting the journey.

phrases.cultural_note: Use this in tuk-tuks, taxis, and buses.
phrases.usage_tips: Point or say this slightly before your actual stop.

phrases.pronunciation: ma-ma yan-na o-ni / naan sel-la vi-rum-bu-gi-ren
phrases.cultural_note: Have your destination written or saved on your phone.
phrases.usage_tips: Use with taxi or tuk-tuk drivers.

phrases.pronunciation: mi-te-ra-ya yo-dan-na pu-lu-wan-da / meet-ta-rai pa-yan-pa-dut-tha mu-di-yu-maa
phrases.cultural_note: Many taxis in Colombo have meters. Insist on using it.
phrases.usage_tips: Say this before starting the ride, or negotiate a fixed price.

phrases.cultural_note: Useful if you need the driver to wait while you run an errand.
phrases.usage_tips: Agree on waiting charges beforehand.

phrases.cultural_note: Simple affirmation. Often accompanied by a head nod.
phrases.usage_tips: Use for confirmation or agreement.

phrases.cultural_note: Direct 'no' can seem rude. Use softer phrases when declining.
phrases.usage_tips: Be polite when refusing. Smile and say thank you.

phrases.cultural_note: Universal acknowledgment. Used very frequently in conversation.
phrases.usage_tips: Perfect for acknowledging what someone said.

phrases.cultural_note: Honesty is appreciated when you don't know something.
phrases.usage_tips: Use when asked a question you can't answer.

phrases.cultural_note: Indirect way of saying things aren't certain.
phrases.usage_tips: Use when you're unsure about plans or answers.

phrases.pronunciation: o-yaa-ge na-ma mo-kad-da / un-gal pe-yar en-na
phrases.cultural_note: Asking names is common when making new friends.
phrases.usage_tips: Use this to introduce yourself and make connections.

phrases.cultural_note: Introduce yourself after asking someone's name.
phrases.usage_tips: Follow with your name clearly pronounced.

phrases.pronunciation: o-yaa-wa mu-na-ga-si-ma sa-thu-thak / un-ga-lai san-dhith-thu ma-ghizh-chi
phrases.cultural_note: Polite way to end introductions.
phrases.usage_tips: Use after exchanging names with someone new.

etiquette_tips.title: Temple Etiquette
dont: Point your feet at Buddha images
Turn your back to Buddha statues

etiquette_tips.title: Greeting Customs
do: Use both hands when giving/receiving items
dont: Use your left hand alone for giving/receiving
Point with one finger (use open hand)

etiquette_tips.title: Dining Etiquette
do: Eat rice and curry with your right hand
Accept second helpings as a compliment
dont: Use your left hand for eating

etiquette_tips.title: General Social Norms
do: Dress modestly, especially outside tourist areas

cultural_notes.title: The Head Wobble
cultural_notes.description: The Sri Lankan head wobble can mean yes, no, maybe, or 'I understand' depending on context. It's a side-to-side tilt, not a shake. Watch locals to understand the meaning!

cultural_notes.title: Time Perception
cultural_notes.description: 'Sri Lankan time' is relaxed. Don't be surprised if things start late or take longer than expected. Embrace the laid-back pace as part of the cultural experience.

cultural_notes.title: Hospitality
cultural_notes.description: Sri Lankans are incredibly hospitable. You may be offered tea or food frequently. Refusing directly can seem rude—accept at least a small amount or explain politely.

cultural_notes.title: Personal Space
cultural_notes.description: Personal space is smaller in Sri Lanka. Don't be surprised by closer conversations or crowded buses. It's normal and not meant to be intrusive.

cultural_notes.title: Language Mix
cultural_notes.description: Many Sri Lankans code-switch between Sinhala/Tamil and English. Don't worry if you hear English words mixed into local languages—it's completely normal!

cultural_notes.title: Shoes Off
cultural_notes.description: Always remove shoes before entering homes, temples, and some shops. Look for shoes at the entrance as a cue. Socks are usually acceptable.
